Puzzle 7 · 8 of 10

Which work does a moving card need?

Move the shared card as the user scrolls. Defer the read once more, this time to a later phase, and predict which work a frame can reuse.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 4: One frame, from tree to pixels

    Compose makes a frame in three phases, always in this order. Composition runs what's marked and updates the tree of nodes. Layout passes constraints down, measures each child once within them, lets each parent pick its own size, then places each child relative to its parent. Drawing has each node paint itself onto a canvas. Each phase can be skipped when its inputs didn't change.

    Review puzzle 4

  • Puzzle 6: Who read the bookmark count?

    The group that runs again is the one where the state read happened, not the one that shows the value. Pass the state object, or a lambda that reads it, down to the composable that needs the value, and a change marks only that composable. That's deferring a read.

    Review puzzle 6

The problem

Puzzle 6 deferred a read from a parent into the child that needs the value. Now a card on the same screen slides down as you scroll. Its text and size stay the same; only its position changes, on every frame of the scroll. Running composition for each of those frames is work nobody sees. Can the read move somewhere cheaper than composition?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Puzzle 4 split every frame into three phases: composition, layout (measure, then place) and drawing. Puzzle 2's state reads are noted per phase: Compose records which phase was running when the value was read, and a change reruns that phase onward, not everything.

The first version reads the position at the top of the composable. The position is an integer number of pixels:

val y = position.value                       // read in composition
Box(modifier = Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x = 0, y = y) }) {
    Text("Saved item")
}

position.value is evaluated while the composable runs, so the read belongs to composition. Every scroll step marks composition, and the frame then measures, places and draws again.

The second version reads it inside the lambda that Modifier.offset { } takes. Compose calls that lambda during placement, so that's where the read happens:

Box(modifier = Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x = 0, y = position.value) }) {
    Text("Saved item")   // read in placement
}

Now a scroll step reruns placement only. Composition doesn't run, and measuring doesn't either: Android's docs note that measuring and placing have separate restart scopes, so a read during placement doesn't redo the measuring before it. The card keeps its size and moves. It's the same idea as puzzle 6, deferring a read, but to a later phase instead of a smaller group.

The same works one phase further. If a value only changes paint, such as a background colour that follows the scroll, read it inside a drawing lambda:

Box(modifier = Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(color.value) })

drawBehind runs its lambda while drawing, so a change of colour reruns drawing alone. Choose the phase by the work your value actually drives.

Go deeperMove versus measure
Why might a card changing its height need more work than a card moving down?

A different height needs the card measured again, and its parent may then move the items below it. Moving a card of the same size reuses its measured size and only places it again.

Back to the main puzzle

The analogy

The theatre once more. If the stage manager rewrites the script every time a prop must slide a little further across the stage, rehearsals never end. The tape marks on the floor (placement) can move without touching the script, and a change of light colour (drawing) needs neither the script nor the tape.

Check yourself

The card now also grows taller as you scroll, and its height follows the same position. Can placement alone handle that change?

Not quite. The offset lambda only moves the card; a height change has to be measured. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Size changes need measuring; position changes don't.

Not quite. Drawing paints what layout decided; it doesn't choose sizes. Re-read that part ↑

Why does reading position.value inside the offset lambda keep composition from running on scroll?

Not quite. The card does move: the change reruns placement.

Not quite. It does track them, in the phase where the lambda runs. Re-read that part ↑

Right. The read is noted where it happens.

A header's background colour follows the scroll, read inside drawBehind. The colour changes. What runs?

Not quite. A colour doesn't change any size or position. Re-read that part ↑

Right. A read during drawing reruns drawing.

Not quite. A change reruns the phase where the read happened. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • Android Developers: Jetpack Compose phases ("When you read the value of a snapshot state during one of the phases listed previously, Compose automatically tracks what it was doing when it read the value."; "Key Point: The measurement step and the placement step have separate restart scopes, meaning that state reads in the placement step don't re-invoke the measurement step before that."; "The value of firstVisibleItemScrollOffset changes every frame during scroll, and by deferring the state read to the layout phase, you can avoid recompositions all along.")
  • Android Developers: Follow best practices ("By switching to the lambda version of the modifier, you can make sure the function reads the scroll state in the layout phase."; "To improve this, use a lambda-based modifier—in this case, drawBehind.")

What you now know

A state read is noted in the phase that makes it. Read a scroll position at the top of a composable and every change reruns composition, layout and drawing. Read it inside the offset lambda, which runs during placement, and a change only moves the card. A value that only changes paint, read inside a drawing lambda, reruns drawing alone.
